t.3.62.1: Having heard those words of the caravan leader, she of faultless limbs, longing to see her husband, then went along with him.
t.3.62.3: The merchants saw a delightful place with abundant fodder and firewood, rich in many roots and fruits, and filled with flocks of various birds.
t.3.62.2: Then, after a long time, in that vast and dreadful forest, they came upon a great lake, lovely on every side, filled with lotuses and fragrant water lilies.
t.3.62.4: Seeing that lake of sweet, pure water, charming and bringing comfort, they, whose beasts of burden were utterly exhausted, set their minds on making camp there.
t.3.62.5: With the consent of the caravan leader, they entered that excellent forest; and the very great caravan, having reached the western hour of the day, made camp there.
t.3.62.6: Then, at the hour of midnight, when all was soundless and still, and the weary caravan lay asleep, a herd of elephants came to a mountain stream, muddied by the flow of their rut-fluid, in search of water.
t.3.62.7: Blocking the path to the lotus pond, the herd suddenly trampled the excellent caravan as it lay sound asleep, the sleepers writhing upon the surface of the earth.
t.3.62.8: Crying out in distress, the caravan merchants, blinded by sleep, ran toward the forest thickets seeking refuge out of great fear; some men were killed by tusks, some by trunks, and some by feet.
t.3.62.9: Then that caravan, full of cattle, donkeys, camels and horses and crowded with people on foot, ran about stricken with fear, its members trampling and striking one another.
t.3.62.10: Letting out dreadful cries, they fell to the surface of the earth; others, caught on trees, were crushed, and some fell into rough ravines. Thus that whole prosperous circle of the caravan was destroyed.
t.3.62.11: Then, when the next day had come, the people who had survived emerged from the forest thicket, grieving over the slaughter that had been wrought and mourning brother, father, son and friend, O lord of men.
t.3.62.12: There Vaidarbhī lamented: "What evil deed have I done, that even this sea of people which I had come upon in the desolate forest has been slain by a herd of elephants, through my own ill fortune alone?"
t.3.62.13: Surely, without doubt, long-lasting sorrow is yet to be endured by me; for no one dies before his time has come: such is the teaching of the elders that I have heard.
t.3.62.14: Wretched as I am, I was not crushed today by the herd of elephants; for nothing befalls men in this world that is not brought about by fate.
t.3.62.15: Not even in my childhood have I done any wrong, by deed, by thought, or by word, that this sorrow should have come upon me.
t.3.62.16: I think that the guardians of the worlds who had assembled for the sake of my svayaṃvara, those deities whom I rejected there for Nala's sake, must surely be the power by which I have come to this separation.
t.3.62.17: Having lamented such sorrows as these, that excellent woman, O tiger among kings, then went on together with the brahmins learned in the Vedas who had survived the slaughter, wholly given over to grief and sorrow.
t.3.62.18: Journeying on, after a long time she reached at evening the great city of Subāhu, the truthful-speaking king of the Cedis, and, wrapped in half of her cut garment, she entered that finest of cities.
t.3.62.19: The townspeople saw her, pale, emaciated and wretched, her hair loosened and her body unwashed, walking along as if she were mad.
t.3.62.20: Seeing her then entering the city of the king of the Cedis, the young sons of the villagers followed her out of curiosity.
t.3.62.21: Surrounded by them, she came near the king's palace. The queen mother, standing on the terrace of the palace, saw her surrounded by the people.
t.3.62.22: Having held back that crowd and brought Damayantī up to the excellent palace terrace, she, filled with wonder, O king, questioned her.
t.3.62.23: Even though you are possessed by sorrow, you bear a supreme form; you shine like lightning among the clouds. Tell me, who are you, and whose are you?
t.3.62.24: Your form is surely not human, even though it is bereft of ornaments; and though you are without companions, you do not fear men, O you whose radiance is like that of the immortals.
t.3.62.25: Having heard those words of hers, Bhaimī spoke these words: "Know me to be a human woman, devoted to my husband."
t.3.62.26: A sairandhrī of good birth, a serving-woman who dwells wherever she pleases, alone, living on fruits and roots, and taking shelter wherever evening finds her.
t.3.62.27: My husband is possessed of countless virtues and is ever devoted to me; and I too, like a shadow, never depart from that heroic husband.
t.3.62.28: By fate, he became excessively attached to gambling; defeated at dice, he went alone to the forest.
t.3.62.29: Consoling my husband, that hero clad in a single garment, distraught as if he were mad, I followed him into the forest.
t.3.62.31: Following him, clad in a single garment, naked, maddened, his mind gone, I never sleep through the many nights.
t.3.62.30: Once in the forest, on some occasion, that hero, tormented by hunger and deeply dejected, cast away even that one garment of his.
t.3.62.32: Then, after a long time had passed, he left me somewhere as I slept, and, cutting off half of my garment, he abandoned me, though I was blameless.
t.3.62.33: Searching for that husband of mine, burning with grief through days and nights, I do not find my beloved, godlike lord, the master of my life and wealth.
t.3.62.34: To her, Bhaimī, distressed, her eyes brimming with tears and lamenting much in this way, the king's mother, herself even more distressed, spoke.
t.3.62.35: Stay with me, fair lady; I feel affection for you. My men will search for your husband, good lady.
t.3.62.36: Or else he himself might come here, wandering hither and thither; living right here, good lady, you will find your husband.
t.3.62.37: Having heard the words of the king's mother, Damayantī spoke these words: "On one condition I am willing to dwell with you, O mother of heroes."
t.3.62.38: I would never eat leftover food, nor would I wash anyone's feet, nor would I speak with other men in any way at all.
t.3.62.39: If any man should solicit me, that man should be punished by you. But for the sake of searching for my husband, I would see brāhmaṇas.
t.3.62.40: If it is to be done thus here, I shall stay without doubt; otherwise, the thought of dwelling here finds no place anywhere in my heart.
t.3.62.41: With a delighted mind the king's mother said this to her: "I shall do all this. Fortunate it is that your vow is of such a kind."
t.3.62.42: Having thus spoken to Bhaimī, O lord of the people, the queen mother then said this to her daughter named Sunandā, O Bhārata:
t.3.62.43: Sunandā, know this godlike woman as a sairandhrī; rejoice in her company yourself, with a mind free from anxiety.
